body_markdown:
When one child plays a sport, it can create a surprising amount of gear. Add in a sibling’s sports equipment, overlapping seasons, duffle bags, gymnastics mats, hockey equipment, volleyball nets, dance costumes, golf travel cases, cleats, helmets, and folding chairs, and the garage starts doing triple duty as a parking spot, equipment room, and lost-and-found.


A seasonal sports equipment rotation can help bring some order back. Keep the gear your family uses this season at home and easy to grab. Clean and dry off-season items can move out of the way until their season returns. For families with a larger collection, a[5×10 storage unit](https://www.publicstorage.com/size-guide/5x10-storage-unit/5x10-storage-unit.html) can work like an off-season locker room for eligible gear and bulky extras.


## Key Takeaways


- Keep in-season gear at home where it’s easy to grab for practices, games, and tournament weekends.
- Clean and air out equipment before putting it away for an extended period.
- Sort gear by sport, athlete, and season so it’s easier to find later.
- Use labeled bins for smaller items and larger bags for bulky equipment.
- A 5×10 storage unit can offer extra room for clean, completely dry off-season gear, depending on facility rules and household needs.


## Start With What’s Taking Over the Garage


Before setting up a system to[store your sporting equipment](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/organizing/how-to-keep-a-sports-season-from-taking-over-your-house.html) , take a look at what’s actually there. For instance, a hockey bag may be taking up a whole corner. A gymnastics mat may be leaning against the wall. Softball gear may be piled beside soccer cleats.


Take stock of the sports equipment taking over the garage, then sort everything into three groups:


**Equipment Group** **What Belongs There**


In season Gear used for current practices, games, lessons, or tournaments


Coming up next Equipment for a sport starting soon


Off season Gear that won’t be used for several months


Once you can more easily see what’s being used right now, what’s coming up, and what won’t be used for a while, the next step gets much easier. Give the first two groups a spot close to home, then move the third group out of the everyday shuffle.


**Keep at home:** Equipment used this week, plus anything for the next sport on the calendar.


**Rotate out:** Clean, completely dry off-season gear that won’t be used for several months.


Making this distinction can keep every sport from claiming a permanent corner of the garage.


## Build a Seasonal Sports Equipment Rotation


A sports equipment rotation works best when it follows your family’s actual calendar, not a generic schedule. Some kids play one sport all year. Others move from soccer to track to softball with barely enough time to locate the next pair of cleats.


Use a paper calendar, shared note, or whiteboard to map out what’s active now, what they’ll need next, and what can wait.


**Time of Year** **Keep Nearby** **Rotate Out**


Fall Soccer gear, football pads, cheer items, field hockey sticks Swim gear, softball bags, golf travel cases


Winter Hockey bags, basketball gear, dance costumes, indoor training equipment Outdoor fall gear and summer sports equipment


Spring Softball or baseball bags, lacrosse gear, soccer equipment, tennis racquets Hockey gear, winter sports equipment, and indoor training items


Summer Swim gear, golf bags, camp equipment, travel-sports bags, softball or baseball gear School-year equipment that isn’t in use


Every family’s lineup looks different. The goal is simply to keep the active gear from competing with every sport your household has ever played.


## Clean Sports Gear Before It Goes Into Storage


Sports equipment earns its mess. Muddy cleats, grass-stained uniforms, sweaty pads, dusty golf bags, and chalky gymnastics grips are all part of the deal. They just shouldn’t go directly into a long-term bin or off-season bag.


Before[rotating gear out](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/seasonal/seasonal-sports-storage-from-baseball-bats-to-snowboards.html) :


- Empty bags and check every pocket.
- Brush off dirt, grass, chalk, and loose debris.
- Wash uniforms and soft items according to their care instructions.
- Let every item dry completely before packing it away.
- Set aside damaged items that may need repair or replacement before the next season.


A little cleanup now can make the first practice of the next season far less chaotic.


## How to Store Sports Equipment for Multiple Kids


A[family sports system](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/storage-tips/smart-storage-solutions-for-your-kids-sports-gear.html) doesn’t require matching containers or a label-maker marathon. It works best when each sport has one obvious home.


Organize by sport first, then by athlete when siblings play the same activity. A labeled bin can hold smaller items, while larger bags can stay with bulky gear.


**Sport or Activity** **Helpful Storage Setup**


Hockey or figure skating Large equipment bag plus a bin for tape, laces, guards, and smaller accessories


Football or lacrosse Bag or tote for pads, helmet accessories, and practice gear


Cheer, dance, or gymnastics Lidded bin for uniforms, shoes, bows, costumes, and performance extras


Soccer or field hockey Tote for cleats, shin guards, sticks, balls, and practice items


Baseball or softball Bat bag with a separate bin for helmets, gloves, and training gear


Volleyball, tennis, or golf Gear bag or travel case with smaller accessories grouped in one pouch


Swim Mesh bag or lidded bin for suits, goggles, towels, and meet supplies


When a season returns, each athlete has one place to check instead of asking where their other cleat, glove, or ball went five minutes before leaving.


## Use a 5×10 Storage Unit as an Off-Season Locker Room


For families whose garage is already full of cars, bikes, tools, and everyday household items, a 5×10 storage unit can offer extra room for eligible off-season sports gear.


A 5×10 unit may work well for stacked bins, folding chairs, golf travel cases, clean equipment bags, and other completely dry items that don’t take part in your daily routine. Clean and air out equipment before packing it away, then confirm current facility rules before storing it.


A simple layout can help:


- Keep one aisle open from the door to the back.
- Group bins by sport or season.
- Label the front and side of each bin.
- Place heavier items lower and lighter items higher.
- Keep a note on your phone listing what’s inside.


[Unit sizes](https://www.publicstorage.com/size-guide) , features, availability, and facility rules vary by location, so check current options before reserving.


## Make the Switch Between Seasons Easier


The end of one season is a good time to prepare for the next. Before putting gear away, make a quick note of anything that could use attention later.


Maybe a helmet needs a new strap. Maybe a dance costume is getting small. Maybe the hockey bag has reached the point where nobody wants to sit next to it in the car.


Keep one short note for each sport with items to repair, replace, or bring out next season. When the calendar starts filling up again, you’ll have fewer surprises and more time to find the snacks before practice.


## FAQs About Sports Equipment Storage


**How do I organize sports equipment for multiple kids?**


Sort equipment by sport, then separate it by athlete when appropriate. Keep in-season gear accessible at home and rotate clean, dry off-season gear into labeled bins, bags, or an eligible storage area.


**How do I store hockey or figure-skating equipment in the off-season?**


Empty the bag, clean equipment according to manufacturer guidance, and let every item dry completely before packing it away. Keep smaller accessories together so they are easier to find before the next season.


**What size storage unit is good for sports equipment?**


A 5×10 unit can be a practical option for families storing clean, dry off-season equipment, stacked bins, folding chairs, and sports bags. The right size depends on how much gear your household has and what else you plan to store.


**Where should I store sports equipment when the garage is full?**


A dry indoor area, basement, closet, or eligible storage unit can help keep off-season gear out of the garage. Keep current-season equipment at home where it’s easy to access.


## Keep the Gear, Get Back the Garage


Sports may be a major part of family life, but every bag, pad, stick, travel case, costume, and mat doesn’t have to live in the garage all year.


A seasonal rotation gives active gear a place to stay ready and off-season equipment a place to wait. That can mean fewer frantic searches, a clearer garage, and a little more breathing room between practices.
